name: Ovagen
summary: A short synthetic peptide from Russian 'bioregulator' research, promoted for the liver and digestive tract; its exact identity and any benefit in people are poorly documented.
what_it_is: Ovagen is one of the short 'bioregulator' peptides associated with Vladimir Khavinson's research group in Russia. An online peptide catalog lists it as a chain of three amino acids, glutamic acid, aspartic acid and leucine (Glu-Asp-Leu, or EDL), but we found no journal article or official register that uses the name Ovagen. A patent from Khavinson's group claims the Glu-Asp-Leu peptide helps the liver regenerate, and the group's lab work suggests short peptides like this act by changing which genes are switched on.

evidence.why: Rat, tissue-culture and cell studies of the Glu-Asp-Leu peptide, plus one small study in people with chronic hepatitis described only in the developer's patent; none of these sources uses the name Ovagen.

status_us.label: Not FDA-approved; not on FDA compounding lists
status_us.note: Ovagen is not an FDA-approved drug and appears on none of FDA's compounding lists (nominated substances, updated May 2026; safety-risk and withdrawn nominations, April 2026). FDA allows pharmacy compounding only from ingredients that are in an approved drug, meet a USP standard, or are on or under review for its bulk list.

benefits.claim: About 75% more dividing liver cells after part of the liver was removed, in rats given the Glu-Asp-Leu peptide
Liver chemistry and stored liver sugar (glycogen) moved back toward normal in rats with chemically induced cirrhosis
Less weakness and pain reported in a small study of 34 people with chronic hepatitis, described only in a patent
Faster growth of rat liver tissue in lab culture
Changed activity of p53, a gene that controls cell death, in aging kidney cell cultures

risks.risk: What products sold as Ovagen contain is unverified: the Glu-Asp-Leu identity comes from an online catalog, and no FDA-approved or compounded version exists
Human safety has not been tested independently; the developers report no toxic effects in mice, rats and guinea pigs

avoid_if: Liver disease such as hepatitis or cirrhosis, unless a clinician is involved

before: General health check, including a liver panel (ALT, AST, bilirubin)
labs.why: No evidence-based monitoring exists for Ovagen; a liver panel is a sensible baseline because liver support is its claimed use.

studies.title: Peptide stimulating regeneration of lever tissue, pharmaceutical composition based thereon and use thereof
studies.people: Rats; the same patent also describes 34 people with chronic hepatitis
studies.finding: In rats, the Glu-Asp-Leu peptide increased liver cell division after partial liver removal and moved liver markers toward normal in cirrhosis. In the human study, most treated patients reported less weakness; the methods are not fully described.

studies.title: Peptide Regulation of Gene Expression: A Systematic Review
studies.people: Cell cultures and DNA in test tubes
studies.finding: A review by the developers of evidence that short peptides bind DNA and change gene activity; the Glu-Asp-Leu peptide changed p53 activity in aging kidney cell cultures.

notes_for_editor: Identity is the main gap: only one online catalog (peptide-db.com, not peer reviewed, and its own references lack identifiers) ties the name Ovagen to Glu-Asp-Leu (EDL). No journal article, MeSH record or Russian register entry using the name Ovagen was found before the session's shared web-search budget ran out. All efficacy and safety data are for the Glu-Asp-Leu peptide, from the developer's Eurasian patent (the Google Patents text was truncated; 'lever' is the patent's own spelling of 'liver'; patent data are not peer reviewed) and a review by the same group, with no independent replication. US status is clear; Russian status of Ovagen was not confirmed.
